title: Coaching is Everything. Coaching is Nothing.
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles, drawing on his own first awful coaching training, asks whether textbook non-directive coaching can improve schools. He concludes it is probably unsustainable and unscalable in a school setting, and offers a lighter style he has seen work: short conversations that ask teachers about their own experience. He gives sample questions for a difficult class, a belief that lessons must be full of engaging activities, and marking workload. His key move is the extreme-position or game-changing question, such as imagining GCSEs did not exist, which frees a teacher from the cage of context. He admits the limitation that good questions depend on the questioner knowing what might work. Most of these questions lead back to the curriculum, which he sees as where most improvement lies.
points: Salles argues formal instructional coaching is likely unsustainable and unscalable in a school and has not yet shown a gain in results or retention.
He recommends 5 to 10 minute conversations with any colleague who voices a problem, with no meetings, timelines or SMART targets.
He claims questions that draw on a teacher's own experience outside school challenge assumptions because context is a cage.
He concedes the weakness that questioners need a lot of knowledge of what works, contrary to the idea that listening alone yields the right question.
His game-changing questions use extreme hypotheticals to push teachers to rethink curriculum, where he says most improvement is found.
quotes: Coaching involves listening 80% of the time. Well, I didn’t know this, and I was full of ‘brilliant’ advice. My feedback was both hilarious and humiliating.

It is also probably completely unsustainable and unscalable in a school. I know lots of people trying to make instructional coaching work in schools, and I’ll be happy to be proved wrong when I see the improvement in Progress 8 or teacher retention.

Any question that helps the teacher focus on how they might improve, based on their own experience, is powerful. Sometimes, mentoring will be much better. But, as you can see from question 5, your questions can still guide the teacher to think about the right things.

These sorts of questions ask us to question our assumptions. They work because they are based on ‘learning’ in the real world, rather than the narrow context of school. Context is a cage, camouflaged as reality.
Many of the questions rely on the experience of the questioner. In other words, you need a lot of knowledge about what might work in order to ask the right question.

This is a huge limitation. No one can pull the best solution out of thin air. Yes, a teacher will always come up with a solution, so coaching will always improve them. But, it will often not be the most efficient, least time-consuming or most impactful.
You will notice that nearly all these questions lead to the curriculum. If coaching is about improvement, the curriculum is where most improvement is to be had.
